title: Book Twelve (1812) — Chapter 9
paragraphs: In the guardhouse where he was taken, the officer and soldiers who had arrested Pierre treated him with hostility, but with respect too. You could still feel in their attitude both doubt about who he might be (perhaps a very important person) and hostility from their recent personal clash with him.

But when the guard was relieved next morning, Pierre felt that he wasn't as interesting to the new guard, officers and men alike, as he had been to his captors. In fact the guard of the second day did not recognize in this big, stout man in a peasant coat the vigorous fellow who had fought so desperately with the marauder and the convoy and had spoken those solemn words about saving a child. They saw in him only No. 17 of the captured Russians, arrested and held for some reason on the orders of the Higher Command. If they noticed anything remarkable about Pierre, it was only his unabashed, thoughtful concentration, and the way he spoke French, which struck them as surprisingly good. Even so, he was put that day with the other arrested suspects, because an officer needed the separate room he had been in.

All the Russians held with Pierre were men of the lowest class. They recognized him as a gentleman and all avoided him, the more so because he spoke French. Pierre felt sad to hear them making fun of him.

That evening he learned that all these prisoners (he among them, probably) were to be tried for arson. On the third day he was taken with the others to a house where a French general with a white mustache sat with two colonels and other Frenchmen with scarves on their arms. With the precision and definiteness usual when addressing prisoners, which is supposed to rule out human frailty, Pierre was questioned like the others about who he was, where he had been, with what purpose, and so on.

These questions, like questions at trials generally, left the essence of the matter aside and shut out any chance of that essence coming to light. They were meant only to form a channel through which the judges wanted the accused's answers to flow, so as to lead to the desired result, namely a conviction. The moment Pierre began to say anything that didn't fit that aim, the channel was removed and the water could run to waste. Pierre also felt what the accused always feel at their trial: bewilderment about why these questions were put to him. He had a feeling that it was only out of condescension, or a kind of politeness, that this device of a channel was used. He knew he was in these men's power, that force alone had brought him there, that force alone gave them the right to demand answers, and that the sole purpose of the gathering was to incriminate him. And so, since they had the power and the wish to incriminate him, the expedient of an inquiry and trial seemed unnecessary. Any answer, clearly, would lead to a conviction. Asked what he was doing when he was arrested, Pierre replied, rather tragically, that he was returning to its parents a child he had saved from the flames. Why had he fought the marauder? Pierre answered that he "was protecting a woman," and that "to protect a woman who was being insulted was the duty of every man; that..." They interrupted him, since this was beside the point. Why was he in the yard of a burning house, where witnesses had seen him? He replied that he had gone out to see what was happening in Moscow. Again they interrupted: they hadn't asked where he was going, but why he was found near the fire. Who was he? they asked, repeating their first question, which he had declined to answer. Again he replied that he couldn't answer it.
"Put that down, that's bad... very bad," said the general with the white mustache and flushed red face, sternly.
On the fourth day fires broke out on the Zubovski rampart.

Pierre and thirteen others were moved to the coach house of a merchant's house near the Crimean bridge. On the way through the streets Pierre felt stifled by the smoke that seemed to hang over the whole city. Fires were visible on all sides. He did not yet understand what the burning of Moscow meant, and he looked at the fires with horror.

He spent four days in the coach house near the Crimean bridge. In that time he learned from the French soldiers' talk that everyone held there was waiting for a decision from the marshal, which might come any day. Pierre couldn't find out from the soldiers which marshal this was. Evidently, to them, "the marshal" stood for a very high and rather mysterious power.
Those first days, before the eighth of September when the prisoners were brought up for a second examination, were the hardest of all for Pierre.
